text: school had been making all night compressed into silence. David's kicks traveled through it in short concussive thuds, rhythmic and close, nearly as present as their own heartbeats. Everything else was stillness and dark and the heavy press of water from every direction. Leon let the flashlight go. He dropped it deliberately, the beam slowly eaten into the black as the current washed it down the hallway. He needed the extra hand to help anchor himself against the wall. Being able to see didn’t matter anymore. Either the wall broke and they wouldn’t need the light, or... He shook the thought off before it finished and turned his focus to the wall at his back and the person beside him. That was the whole job now. Stay still. Stay against the wall. Don't let the current make a decision for either of them. He got his arm around Dwight and pressed them both flat, narrowing the target, willing the water to find something else to pull at. Dwight's hand found his sleeve. The grip was immediate and tight, trembling in small, hiccupped pulses that Leon felt more than registered — every second stretching out longer than it should. He couldn’t reassure the man beyond tightening his own grip, so he just let the hand stay and kept them both against the wall and counted David's kicks moving through the water like a second heartbeat. Dwight held on. He couldn't tell if his eyes were open. The dark was the same either way, complete and total, pressing in from every direction. He didn't fight it. Years of trials had put something in him that wasn't courage exactly but functioned like it in emergencies — a flat, stubborn refusal to spend energy on what couldn't be helped. He was scared. He was tired. He was not particularly strong. But he could be still. He could last, if he stayed calm, if he kept his grip and kept his lungs and didn't think about how much time was passing. He could last. Probably. The movement hit them from the side without warning — a flurry of it, close, maybe two feet away in the dark, turbulent enough that the current shifted and tugged at his legs with new intent. His hand tightened on Leon's sleeve. He felt Leon go rigid beside him. Neither of them reached out. Moving meant opening up to the current. Moving meant losing the wall. Moving meant finding out what that was, and there were only so many things it could be, and none of the options were ones they could think about right now without their bodies making a decision they weren't ready for. They focused instead on the contact points. The texture of sleeves under fingers. The wall against shoulders. David's kicks moving through the water like a pulse. That was everything. That was all there was. They stayed, anchored, and tried not to think about what was happening two feet away from them in the dark. Orela had wrapped her arms around Danny’s chest the moment the ceiling closed in. Now, pressed with her back tight to the wall, face tucked low and leaving small bubbles in his hair, she was holding him there — keeping him still. Danny's hands were clamped over her arms, tight enough to hurt, as if her arms were all that stood between him and the darkness. She could feel the small hitches moving through him at irregular intervals, his body working against the stillness she needed from both of them. She'd registered the wheeze in his breathing before they went under. Had noted it and filed it and told herself it was manageable. Down here, she could feel it — the shallow quality of what he'd managed to grab before the water took the last of the air, the way each hitch cost him more than it should have. Between the injuries from earlier and the exhaustion he hadn’t had nearly as much time as the others to recover from, he hadn’t managed to get a proper breath before going under. She held him tighter and kept still and counted David's kicks moving through the water and tried not to let her hands shake. Her own lungs flared hot in her chest, but she focused only on him. If she could keep him still and calm, they both could make it. Danny knew exactly how much air he had left. That was the problem. In the hallway there hadn't been time to count — just the current and the dark and the animal insistence on the next breath. Down here there was nothing but time and stillness, and he had already gone in shorter than he would have preferred. He tried to be still. Tried to let Orela's grip be the thing doing the work, to stop spending what he had left on anything that wasn't strictly necessary. It almost worked. The need to move started low, barely there, and crept upward with patient incremental certainty until it wasn't a suggestion anymore. He shifted, a small involuntary thing, trying to suppress what was building in his chest, and felt Orela's arms tighten in response. Her palm pressed flat against his sternum. Taking inventory. He felt her go still in a different way — the careful conservation of before replaced by the specific stillness of someone who had suddenly understood something. His grip shifted on her arms without meaning to, fingers searching for leverage, and the thought that arrived alongside it was not a thought so much as a demand. Up. She felt it in his hands before he'd finished processing it. He fought it. That was the thing — he knew what was happening, could name it with the specific clarity that made it worse, and fought it anyway.
